says.text: As a private clinic operations manager, I need a reliable way to ensure patients know what to do after they leave the appointment.
Our doctors should not have to manually chase every follow-up, reminder, and patient question.
Administrators need to see only the post-visit cases that actually require action.
We need a process that works between visits without forcing us to replace our medical information system.

thinks.text: Important follow-up steps can be missed when instructions are split between the doctor, administrator, and patient.
If a patient’s condition worsens or they do not complete a control procedure, the clinic should identify that signal early.
A clear patient journey after the visit would make our service feel more coordinated and trustworthy.
Any new workflow must fit the clinic’s existing operations and use only the data needed for follow-up.

does.text: Coordinates how doctors and administrators communicate post-visit instructions and follow-up responsibilities.
Reviews patient complaints, missed control appointments, and cases where patients return without completing recommended actions.
Asks administrators to remind patients about procedures, tests, or repeat consultations when there is no consistent automated process.
Looks for operational tools that can organize patient follow-up while remaining separate from the clinic’s core medical system.

feels.text: Concerned that patients may be left without clear guidance after an appointment.
Frustrated when staff spend time sorting routine reminders from issues that need clinical attention.
Responsible for maintaining a consistent patient experience across doctors and administrative staff.
Cautious about introducing a new system that could create additional work or disrupt established processes.

pains.text: Post-visit responsibilities are fragmented, so it is unclear who should communicate each next step to the patient.
Patients may forget or misunderstand follow-up instructions, control procedures, and timing between appointments.
Doctors and administrators can be overwhelmed by routine follow-up messages instead of focusing on meaningful patient signals.
The clinic lacks a structured way to collect information about a patient’s wellbeing after the visit and escalate concerning responses.
Connecting new processes to an existing medical information system can be difficult when only limited data is needed.

gains.text: Every patient receives a clear, understandable plan of next actions immediately after the visit.
Patients receive timely reminders for control procedures, tests, and follow-up appointments.
Clinic staff receive a focused queue of cases that need attention rather than handling every routine interaction manually.
The clinic can monitor patient wellbeing between visits and respond earlier when a reported issue requires action.
A standalone follow-up workflow can be introduced with minimal dependence on the existing medical information system.

options.title: Subscription · CareRoute
options.audience: Private clinic operations managers at multi-specialty clinics that need a standardized post-visit workflow without replacing their medical information system
options.value_proposition: A predictable monthly platform gives clinics clear patient action plans, automated follow-ups, and an exception-only staff queue that reduces missed care steps and routine manual chasing.

options.time_to_value: 30 minutes to enroll the first patient in a follow-up pathway
options.score_rationale: This lowers the adoption barrier for smaller, variable-volume clinics and makes first use easy to test. However, care follow-up is not inherently a transaction marketplace, and per-pathway pricing can create budget uncertainty and weaker recurring revenue predictability.

options.description: The clinic pays an implementation and workflow-design retainer plus an ongoing SaaS fee for configurable care pathways, staff training, escalation rules, reporting, and optional limited MIS data connection. architecture.epicenter_rationale: The primary innovation is concentrated in the value_propositions section: a standalone post-visit continuity layer that converts clinical instructions into patient action plans, reminders, wellbeing check-ins, and an exception-only staff queue. Key resources, activities, integrations, and customer relationships are structured mainly to deliver this coordinated follow-up offer without requiring replacement of the clinic’s core medical information system.
architecture.pattern_rationale: The canvas unbundles post-visit patient relationship and coordination work from the clinic’s core clinical-system and appointment operations. The standalone platform takes responsibility for routine communication, pathway completion, and initial signal triage, while clinicians and administrators retain responsibility for escalated cases; optional MIS connections provide data support rather than making the product a multi-sided platform. Revenue streams are clinic-paid subscription, usage, and managed-service fees, with no free segment or partner-led open-innovation model.

hypotheses.text: In interviews and workflow walkthroughs with 15 operations managers at private multi-specialty clinics, at least 10 will identify fragmented post-visit ownership as a top-3 operational problem and agree to run a 30-day pilot of a structured follow-up pathway; the hypothesis is false if fewer than 10 do so.

In a 30-day pilot covering at least 100 enrolled patients, at least 70% of patients will open their post-visit action plan and at least 60% will complete or explicitly respond to one scheduled follow-up action; the hypothesis is false if either threshold is missed.

At least 6 of 10 qualified private clinics that complete a product demo and receive a proposal for a standalone subscription priced at $1,000 per month will sign a paid 3-month pilot or annual subscription; the hypothesis is false if fewer than 6 sign.

Among clinics that complete a paid pilot, the median operations manager will estimate that the exception-only queue reduces administrator time spent on routine follow-up reminders by at least 30% versus the prior manual process; the hypothesis is false if the median reduction is below 30%.

In 2 pilot clinics, a clinic administrator can launch one approved post-visit pathway without MIS integration, enrolling the first 20 patients and scheduling their reminders within 1 business day after receiving a 60-minute onboarding session; the hypothesis is false if either clinic cannot meet this result.

For 100 test patient responses across 3 clinic-approved pathways, the configured escalation rules will route at least 95% of predefined concerning or overdue responses to the correct staff queue and will create an auditable timestamped record for 100% of routed cases; the hypothesis is false if either threshold is not achieved.

says.text: As the owner of a vintage automobile, I need a workshop that understands my exact model rather than treating it like a modern car.
I cannot risk handing this rare engine or transmission to a mechanic who has never worked on one.
Finding a specialist takes more time than finding the actual replacement part.
I want to know upfront whether a workshop has the tools, manuals, and experience for this specific repair.

thinks.text: As a vintage automobile owner, I worry that an incorrect repair could damage an irreplaceable component.
A nearby workshop is not useful if it lacks experience with my car's rare model and mechanical systems.
I need credible proof of prior work on the same model, engine, gearbox, or electrical system.
I may need to travel or arrange transport for the car, so choosing the right specialist the first time matters.

does.text: The vintage automobile owner searches online using the model name together with the faulty component and repair terms.
They ask owner clubs, forums, social-media groups, and acquaintances for recommendations.
They call several workshops to describe the car, verify expertise, and ask whether the workshop will accept the job.
They compare reviews, photos of previous restorations, location, and availability before arranging an inspection.

feels.text: The vintage automobile owner feels anxious because the car may be harmed by an inexperienced mechanic.
They feel frustrated by vague workshop claims of being able to repair any car.
They feel overwhelmed by conflicting recommendations from communities and online search results.
They feel protective of a car that has personal, historical, or collector value.

pains.text: The vintage automobile owner cannot easily identify workshops that genuinely specialize in their exact rare model.
They struggle to verify whether a mechanic has experience with a particular old engine, transmission, carburetor, electrical system, or other specific unit.
General search results and directories do not clearly show model-specific expertise, suitable equipment, or past repair work.
They waste time contacting workshops that later decline the job or reveal that they lack relevant knowledge.
A wrong diagnosis or improper repair can lead to costly damage, delays, and difficulty sourcing replacement parts.

gains.text: The vintage automobile owner can quickly find workshops matched to their precise car model and faulty mechanical unit.
They can see trustworthy evidence of relevant specialist experience, such as completed work on comparable vehicles or components.
They can contact suitable workshops with confidence that the repair request is within their capabilities.
They reduce the risk of avoidable damage and improve the chance of a correct, durable repair.
They save time and can make an informed choice even when the best specialist is outside their immediate area.

options.title: Subscription · Heritage Workshop Finder
options.audience: Owners of vintage and rare automobiles seeking verified specialists for a specific model, engine, gearbox, carburetor, or electrical system
options.value_proposition: A paid membership gives collectors verified, model-specific workshop matches and proof of relevant repair experience before they risk their car.
options.description: Owners pay a subscription for unlimited access to a searchable, verified directory of workshops, specialist profiles, completed-work evidence, and fit-for-job matching. It directly addresses pain 1 and pain 2—difficulty identifying and verifying true model- and component-specific expertise—and supports gains 1 and 2 by helping owners quickly find matched workshops with credible evidence. The recurring value is strongest for active restorers, collectors with multiple vehicles, and owners managing ongoing maintenance.
options.time_to_value: 20 minutes to first verified workshop shortlist
options.score_rationale: Strong fit because trust, verification, and repeated specialist discovery directly reduce the owner's risk of costly incorrect repairs. The score is constrained by the relatively niche and episodic nature of repair needs, which can increase churn for single-car owners.

options.title: Transaction Fee · RareRepair Match

options.value_proposition: Owners can submit one detailed repair request and securely book a qualified specialist, avoiding wasted calls and unsuitable workshops.
options.description: The platform takes a fee from the confirmed inspection or repair booking, or charges the owner a booking service fee, after matching the vehicle, component, and repair need with an accepting workshop. This tackles pain 4—time wasted contacting workshops that decline work—and pain 5—the cost of wrong diagnosis or improper repair—while delivering gains 3 and 4 through confident contact and a better chance of a durable repair. Model-specific intake details and workshop acceptance make the transaction meaningful rather than simply selling a directory listing.
options.time_to_value: 48 hours to first workshop acceptance or inspection offer
options.score_rationale: This is the strongest option because revenue occurs at the moment the owner receives high-stakes value: a credible specialist willing to take the job. Its main challenge is operational complexity, including workshop supply, variable repair quotes, and potential disputes around repair outcomes.

options.title: Retainer Plus SaaS · Heritage Shop Signal
options.audience: Specialist vintage-car workshops serving owners of rare models and legacy mechanical or electrical systems
options.value_proposition: A workshop SaaS and lead-management service turns documented model-specific expertise into qualified repair requests from owners who need exactly that capability.
options.description: Specialist workshops pay a monthly retainer plus SaaS fee for a verified expertise profile, model/component capability catalog, repair-portfolio publishing, qualified-request intake, and lead qualification tools. It supports owners' pain 1 and pain 3 by making genuine specialization, equipment, and prior work visible, and enables gains 2 and 3 through credible evidence and confident outreach. Workshops benefit by receiving better-qualified jobs instead of broad, poorly matched inquiries, while the marketplace gains the structured data needed for precise matching.
options.time_to_value: 7 days to publish a verified capability profile and receive the first qualified request
options.score_rationale: This creates more predictable B2B revenue and directly builds the verified supply data that owners need to trust matches. It scores lower than transaction fees because small specialist workshops may resist software adoption or have limited capacity for additional jobs.

architecture.epicenter_rationale: The differentiation is driven jointly by Key Resources and Value Propositions: the verified model- and component-level capability database, matching taxonomy, and trust assets enable evidence-based specialist selection rather than a generic workshop directory. Customer Segments and Channels are also deliberately focused on a narrow rare-vehicle owner niche and marque-club access, while Revenue Streams combine booking fees, owner subscriptions, and workshop SaaS. These coordinated changes make the canvas a coherent multi-epicenter redesign rather than a change to pricing or a single offer alone.
architecture.pattern_rationale: The canvas connects interdependent groups: vintage-car owners submit detailed repair requests and seek verified specialists, while restoration workshops publish capabilities, portfolios, and accept qualified jobs. The Marketplace and SaaS platform in Key Resources, guided request intake in Customer Relationships, and both owner-facing and workshop-facing channels create the exchange mechanism between these groups. If I could compare current readings with normal patterns, I could prioritize my inspections better.

hypotheses.text: At least 40% of 60 history teachers and culturally curious travelers who plan a local outing within the next 90 days will select a route from a clickable prototype within 15 minutes and rate its theme, context, and logistics at 4 or 5 out of 5; the hypothesis is false if fewer than 24 do so.

At least 15% of 100 qualified visitors who complete a route-preview landing-page flow will start a €6/month subscription trial or provide payment authorization for access to vetted map-ready routes; the hypothesis is false if fewer than 15 visitors do so.

At least 8 of 20 interviewed schools, museums, or heritage organizations will agree to pay at least €1,200 per year for a route-authoring license after reviewing a group-route prototype and pricing proposal; the hypothesis is false if fewer than 8 organizations agree.

Using a standard route-authoring workflow and local-expert review, a two-person editorial team can publish 20 routes with at least 5 stops each in 30 days, while at least 90% of sampled stop hours, locations, and access notes are verified as accurate; the hypothesis is false if either threshold is missed.

At least 80% of 30 pilot-route users will complete a route without reporting a material sequencing, navigation, or access error, and at least 70% will say the stated duration was within 30 minutes of actual duration; the hypothesis is false if either rate falls below its threshold.

Within one pilot region, at least 10 of 30 contacted guides, museums, and workshop providers will list a route-linked paid experience with a commission of 15% or less and maintain at least 4 bookable dates per month; the hypothesis is false if fewer than 10 providers meet both conditions.

After receiving a post-event report based on at least 100 discovery impressions, at least 12 of 20 repeat organizers (60%) will state that the theme, time, or location insight changed a decision for their next event; fewer than 12 would falsify the claim that attendance analytics solve a meaningful programming problem.

At least 10 of 20 repeat organizers who receive at least 10 platform-attributed bookings or verified attendees in a month will choose a paid organizer plan at a price of €29 per month or more within 30 days; fewer than 10 conversions would falsify the subscription revenue assumption.

For at least 90% of 50 organizer-submitted events, the platform can validate mandatory fields—date, time, venue, category, capacity, and ticket link—and publish the listing within 24 hours without manual data correction; a rate below 90% would falsify the promised self-service time to value.

At least 8 of 20 organizers posting a request for an artist, performer, or collaborator will receive 3 or more relevant artist responses within 14 days; fewer than 8 successful requests would falsify the near-term usefulness of artist matching, although the core event-discovery model could still operate without it.

At least 40% of users who complete a first workout will complete 8 or more workouts during the following 28 days when offered reminders, gradual progression, and low-pressure tracking; retention below 40% falsifies the assumption that the product can establish a repeatable beginner habit sufficient to support subscription retention.

At least 70% of new users who report limited time, low energy, or a missed workout will choose and complete a 5–10 minute simplified routine rather than abandon the session when that option is presented; a rate below 70% falsifies the importance of adaptive short routines as a reliable recovery mechanism.

For 90% or more of users who report knee, wrist, or back discomfort during onboarding, the workout-planning system will return a clinically approved substitute routine in under 2 seconds with no excluded movement included; performance below 90% falsifies the operational feasibility of personalized low-impact alternatives.

At least 10% of active monthly users will book and pay for one optional 15-minute coach form-review session within 60 days when sessions cost US$15–25; a booking rate below 10% falsifies the coach-session transaction fee as a meaningful secondary revenue stream.
